title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving slowly, carefully, and with genuine relish through one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss is a novel about memory, family, and the terrible costs of growing up in a world that has very fixed ideas about who you are allowed to become.
At its centre is Maggie Tulliver — brilliant, ardent, and perpetually at odds with almost everything her world expects of her.
Today we begin where the novel asks us to begin: with the shadow of the mill itself — family, duty, and the love that binds even as it constrains.
I'm joined by three remarkable readers, each of whom brings something quite distinct to this conversation.

Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads George Eliot with the eye of a craftsman — she sees the architecture behind the emotion, and she makes that architecture feel genuinely exciting.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes that great fiction is finally about individual moral character — about goodness, weakness, and what it costs a person to act rightly.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power — who benefits, who is crushed, and whose suffering the social order quietly regards as acceptable.
Eleanor, Edmund, Daniel — welcome, all three of you.

Eleanor, I'd like to start with you, because you've written about the moment in the novel when Maggie sees her father's helplessness — and it seems to me that passage unlocks something essential about what this novel is doing.
Thank you — yes, and I think that passage is remarkable precisely because of what Eliot does with time.
Maggie is a child, and this is a child's moment — and yet the narrator insists it belongs to a category of adult experience that most people reach only much later in life.
The phrase Eliot uses is extraordinary.
"that simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish"
The word "knits" — not bonds, not ties — knits.
It implies something domestic and painstaking and continuous — love as a practice, not a feeling that simply arrives.
And notice that Eliot places the narrator in the first person plural — "knits us," "nearest to us."
She pulls every reader into Maggie's experience, makes it universal — this has happened to you, or it will.
That is a very deliberate and very confident narrative move, and it sets the emotional stakes for everything that follows.
Eleanor is right to dwell on that word "primitive," I think, because it carries the novel's deepest argument.
Eliot is not using it pejoratively — she means something closer to foundational, elemental.
This is the love that precedes all calculation, all resentment, all the accumulated grievances of family life.
And it is precisely that love which makes Maggie's situation so painful throughout the novel.
She cannot simply reason herself free of her father and her brother, however much they constrain her, because this bond is prior to reason.
We see this again with the father himself, near the end — and there is a line of Mr Tulliver's that I find almost unbearable in its simplicity.
"we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me"
There is no anger left in him there, no accusation — only exhaustion, and a kind of battered tenderness toward his wife.
That line does more for his character than pages of description could.
I want to hold onto what Edmund said about that exhaustion — because the question the novel keeps pressing is: what has exhausted him, and why?
"This world's been too many for me" — the world, not a person, not bad luck.
Tulliver is a man destroyed by a legal and financial system he never had the means to navigate — and the Tullivers' ruin is entirely legible as a class story.

But here is what makes the novel genuinely complex: that primitive love Eleanor identified, that foundational bond Edmund speaks of, becomes the very instrument through which the family's humiliation is reproduced.
Look at what Tom does with it.

"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both"
Tom weaponises the family's love and suffering — uses their father's dying wish, the sacrifices made — as a cudgel against his sister's autonomy.
The bond that should shelter Maggie becomes the mechanism of her enclosure.
Eliot is clear-eyed about this — she loves the Tullivers and she indicts them simultaneously.
Daniel, that phrase — "shelter" becoming "enclosure" — is exactly the double movement that Eliot builds into every major scene involving the Tulliver family.
And what strikes me technically is how the Bible-oath scene is staged.
Tom says, "Do what I require" — not ask, not request: require.
He is demanding a spoken formula — a liturgical renunciation — as if love itself can be regulated by oath.
The form of the scene mimics a religious rite, and that mimicry is deeply ironic — because what Tom is actually enforcing is respectability, not conscience.
Eliot understands that the machinery of moral language can be entirely captured by social anxiety.
I take Daniel's point about enclosure, and Eleanor's about the irony — though I would resist framing Tom purely as a villain of the piece.
Tom has genuinely sacrificed — he has surrendered his own prospects, his own youth, to honour his father's name.
His tragedy is that he cannot see how his own discipline has calcified into something rigid and punishing.
He has made duty his entire self, and duty without imagination becomes — as Burke might have said — mere compulsion dressed in virtue's clothing.
The pathos of the novel, for me, is that both Tom and Maggie are, in their different ways, destroyed by the same primitive bond — the same love that Eliot shows us so movingly in that early passage.
That seems to me exactly the right place to pause on this opening movement — love as the source of everything both generous and suffocating in this novel.
We've heard Eliot pull readers into Maggie's experience with that first-person plural — the "us" of primitive love.
We've heard a dying man surrender to the world that defeated him with a line of heartbreaking plainness.
And we've seen how Tom Tulliver can turn that same family love into something that closes around Maggie like a fist.
In our next segment, we'll press deeper into that world — the Dodsons, the Tullivers, and the social codes that govern life on the Floss.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Maggie's Hunger: Mind Against the World

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're inside one of the novel's most quietly devastating territories — the education of Tom and Maggie Tulliver.
Two children, the same household, utterly different minds — and a world determined to reward only one of them.
To help us think through what George Eliot is doing here, I'm joined by three remarkable readers.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose gift is seeing exactly how a great writer builds her effects — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral adventures — stories of character tested by circumstance, of goodness and weakness measured against the world.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees every institution in a novel — school, family, law — as a mechanism of power, and every marginalised figure as the clearest evidence of what that power produces.
Let's begin with Tom at Mr. Stelling's — humiliated, desperate, reaching for the only resource he has left.
What strikes me first about that passage is how Eliot complicates Tom before she celebrates Maggie.
Tom is not simply the dull, obstructing brother — not yet, not here.
Eliot gives us something surprisingly tender: a boy whose pride has been entirely stripped away, and who is left with nothing but human sensibility.
And then she does something architecturally brilliant — she turns that humiliation into prayer.
Tom can't improvise in class, he can't improvise socially — and he almost can't improvise spiritually either.
He is so bound by form and precedent that adding a single extempore line to his evening prayers feels like an act of bold transgression.
Listen to what he actually says when he finally dares it — the narrator sets this up with such careful restraint:
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
It's heartbreaking precisely because it's so small — and so earnest.
Quite so — and I think one must resist the temptation to condescend to Tom here, which is a temptation Eliot herself occasionally indulges.
What Eliot is actually rendering is something Johnson would have recognised: the moral weight of honest effort.
Tom is not lazy, not rebellious — he is simply in the wrong place, fitted with the wrong tools.
The prayer is touching because it reveals a character still capable of supplication — still reaching beyond himself for help.
The final petition — asking that Mr. Stelling should simply make him stop doing Euclid — is of course comic.
But comedy in Eliot is rarely decorative; it illuminates character with a precision that pure pathos cannot.
I want to hold onto something Eleanor said — about form and precedent binding Tom so tightly he can barely speak a free sentence even to God.
That is not individual temperament alone — that is a class formation.
Tom has been shaped by a world where inherited custom is the only safe ground — improvisation is for those with the social capital to survive getting it wrong.
Mr. Stelling's school is not educating Tom — it is demonstrating to him, daily, that he belongs to an inferior order.
And Eliot sees this with brutal clarity — which makes it all the more extraordinary that she then cuts immediately to Maggie, who flourishes in exactly the same environment.
That's exactly the turn I wanted to take — because the contrast Eliot sets up when Maggie picks up the Latin Grammar is one of the novel's most charged moments.
Eleanor, can you walk us into it?
With enormous pleasure — because this passage contains one of the finest similes in the whole novel.
Maggie picks up Tom's Latin Grammar not as a duty but as a delight — she goes straight to the examples, skips the rules entirely.
And then Eliot reaches for this image that takes your breath away — she tells us what those fragmentary Latin sentences are like for Maggie:
"These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her imagination."
Strange horns of beasts — that image does something extraordinary to the abstraction of grammar.
It makes language feel like natural history — like specimens from a world you haven't yet reached but desperately want to.
Maggie doesn't just want to learn Latin — she wants the far-off region itself.
The image is superb — and what I find equally notable is the sentence that follows: she is proud because she finds it interesting.
That is a very precise moral observation — the pleasure of legitimate pride in one's own capacity, rather than pride in what one has been given.
Maggie's appetite for knowledge is not vanity — it is a kind of vocation.
But Eliot is also quietly noting a cruel irony: Maggie's vocation has no institutional home.
The very grammar that would be Tom's burden if he could master it is Maggie's joy — and yet the world has decided the grammar belongs to Tom.
That irony is the structural irony of the entire novel — and Eliot won't let us look away from it.
Maggie is described as proud — and that word is doing a great deal of political work.
A girl's intellectual pride in 1830s provincial England is not a safe thing to carry — it has nowhere to go.
And notice what Eliot does at the end of this passage — Tom calls out, and the far-off region vanishes.
It is the novel in miniature: Maggie's imagination interrupted by the claims of a world organised around her brother's needs.
Beautifully put — and that sibship, that binding of Maggie to Tom, runs through everything we're discussing today.
The sword accident — where Tom falls and Maggie believes him dead — is one of the most viscerally tender passages in the book.
Edmund — does that scene change your sense of what Maggie and Tom mean to each other?
It is, to my mind, one of the finest passages of sustained emotional truth in the Victorian novel — and I do not say that lightly.
Eliot renders the horror of the moment — the sword, the faint, the shaking — in extraordinarily compressed prose.
But the line that arrests me comes after the danger has passed:
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
That word yet — it does so much work.
It acknowledges that grief and guilt will come — but insists that love, at its most elemental, is simply gratitude for existence.
That yet is doing the work of an entire psychology — it is the novel's compression at its most ruthless.
What I notice alongside it is the physical detail — Maggie shaking Tom by the collar even as she believes him dead.
Eliot gives us the paradox of helpless love — you shake someone you believe is gone because the body refuses to accept what the mind already fears.
It's psychologically exact in the way that only the greatest novelists manage — not poetic truth but observed truth.
I want to place this scene in the architecture of the novel's argument about Maggie and Tom — because it is not only emotionally devastating, it is structurally necessary.
This is the scene that establishes the full cost of Maggie's love for her brother — a love that will bind and ultimately destroy her.
The depth of her attachment here makes legible everything that follows: every sacrifice, every return, every capitulation to Tom's judgment.
Eliot is not sentimentalising sibling love — she is dissecting it, showing us how love for one person can function as a cage.
That image of the cage will echo through everything that comes later — but before we leave this world of Mr. Stelling's school, I want to turn to Philip Wakem.
Because if Tom represents one kind of limitation on Maggie's hunger, Philip offers something entirely different — a mind that meets hers with genuine recognition.
Daniel — how do you read their first real connection?
Philip Wakem is one of Eliot's most carefully constructed figures of what I'd call compounded exclusion.
He is the son of the lawyer who will ruin Tulliver — already positioned as the enemy's child.
And he is physically disabled — doubly marked by a world that measures worth by strength and lineage.
What Eliot does in these scenes is use Maggie's ease with Philip to reveal the generosity of her intelligence — she does not see the deformity first.

But she also uses Philip's longing for Maggie to reveal the cost of isolation — his question about whether she would love him as a brother is heartbreaking precisely because it is a question he cannot stop himself from asking.
And then Philip tells her something that is as close to a declaration as a boy can make — with a child's honesty that Eliot renders as devastating rather than sweet.
He says — and the passage earns its full weight if you hear it slowly:
"I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you.
And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours."
A sister — not a lover, not even a friend: a sister.
Philip reaches for the one bond he thinks might be permissible — and in doing so reveals exactly what he cannot ask for.
One ought not overlook Maggie's response — which is to offer what she can give: to kiss him as she kisses Tom.
Eliot tells us Maggie is wondering how to convince Philip she could like him just as well, although he was crooked — and then she arrives at an act of pure instinctive grace:
"Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like."
There is no calculation in that offer — only the desire to give what comfort is available.
This is what I mean when I say that Eliot's deepest subject is not society but goodness — the small, inarticulate movements of a generous nature toward those who need it.
Goodness is real — I won't deny that — but Eliot is also showing us something harder here.
Maggie can offer Philip only what she offers Tom — the love of a sister, the bond of childhood innocence.
The world these children inhabit has not yet invented a form for what Philip and Maggie might otherwise be to each other.
Philip is the son of the wrong man; Maggie is the wrong kind of woman — too hungry, too dark-eyed, too much.
Too much — and yet not enough of the right kind, by the world's measure.
We've been tracing today how George Eliot builds Maggie's hunger — through Tom's pain, through the Latin Grammar, through the terror of the sword accident, and through Philip's lonely declaration.
What emerges is a portrait not just of an unusually gifted child, but of a world constitutionally unable to accommodate that gift.
My thanks to Eleanor, Edmund, and Daniel — we'll be back shortly to follow Maggie further into the novel's great reckoning with desire and renunciation.

segments.title: Class and Catastrophe: The Tulliver Collapse

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the Tulliver family's ambitions and anxieties — now we turn to the machinery of their destruction.
This segment is called Class and Catastrophe: The Tulliver Collapse.
With me are three voices who've been thinking hard about these chapters.
Dr Eleanor Hartley reads Eliot as a supreme architect of prose — alert to every structural choice, every ironic pivot.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of someone who believes the novel's deepest subject is individual character under pressure — not social systems.
And Dr Daniel Rosen wants us to see the Tulliver ruin as something the novel's social world actively produces — not merely suffers.
Let's start with the moment the catastrophe becomes real — when Maggie tells Tom what is happening to their father.
Eleanor, that scene is so brief it's almost brutal.
It is brutal, and that's the precise effect Eliot is engineering.
She gives us the narrator's framing first — Maggie is urged to fuller speech by Tom's freedom from apprehension.
"urged to fuller speech by Tom's freedom from apprehension"
That phrase does extraordinary work — Tom's obliviousness is what breaks Maggie open.
And then the sentence Eliot gives her is almost childlike in its simplicity.
"Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left."
Three repetitions of 'he will' — and that final clause, 'nothing left,' landing like a stone.
Eliot could have written this with far greater sophistication, but she didn't — and that restraint is the whole point.
One notices that Maggie doesn't say 'we' — she says 'he will have nothing left.'
The whole of Maggie's character is in that pronoun — her instinct is entirely for her father, not for herself.
This is what I find most compelling about the Tulliver catastrophe — it reveals character, it does not merely illustrate economics.
Mr Tulliver has been hurtling toward this ruin through a series of choices that are wholly his own.
His pride, his stubbornness — these are not imposed upon him by a system; they are him.
I'd push back on that, Edmund — gently but firmly.
Eliot takes considerable care to show us the institutional machinery that chews Tulliver up.
Look at what she says about the law itself — not Tulliver's psychology, the law.
"Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs."
Injured honesty — that phrase is doing everything.
The legal system is structured so that the only way an honest man can win is to hire a more capable knave.
Tulliver's ruin isn't a failure of character — it's what happens when a small man enters a system designed to strip him.
I grant you the observation about the law's structure — Eliot is satirical there, and sharply so.
But Tulliver is not dragged into the cock-fight — he rushes toward it.
Consider his hatred of Wakem — a hatred so elaborate it borders on the operatic.
Eliot's narrator is wonderfully precise about this.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber, — always looking so sure of his game!"
That is free indirect discourse at full stretch — Eliot letting us hear Tulliver's own mental voice, with all its bile intact.
It is comic — but also a self-portrait of a man constructing his own doom.
That passage on Wakem is one of my favourite pieces of Eliotic narration in the whole novel.
There's that magnificent little parenthetical — 'metaphorically speaking' — as if the narrator is slightly embarrassed to be reporting Tulliver's reasoning at all.
And Eliot builds the case — Wakem was at the bottom of Pivart's irrigation, Wakem had tried to make Dix stand out — the accumulation is wickedly funny.
But what strikes me structurally is that the comic register here is doing serious damage to our trust in Tulliver's judgment.
By the time he rushes into law, we already know he cannot see clearly — the comedy has done its work.
Eleanor is right about the comedy — but I want to hold both things at once.
Tulliver's paranoid portrait of Wakem is laughable, yes — but Wakem really is powerful, and the law really does favour him.
The comedy deflects us — as comedy often does — from the structural reality underneath.
And then Eliot turns to the education system — and that satire is if anything even more unsparing.
She sets it up as a historical disclaimer — 'all this happened in those dark ages' — and then eviscerates those dark ages entirely.

"There was but one way of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?"
The market for education is exposed as a protection racket for the credentialled and the connected.
Tom Tulliver is sent to Stelling because his father has no way to distinguish quality — that ignorance is itself a class condition.
The Stelling passage is among the sharpest things Eliot writes in the novel, I'll freely concede that.
Though I notice Eliot's target is not capitalism as such — it is pretension, and incompetence shielded by social convention.
The clergyman-schoolmaster is a comic grotesque, not an emblem of systemic oppression.
She gives us the metaphor of a creature endowed with the power of boring a hole through rock — having no faculty to spare.
That is a portrait of individual limitation, not of structural evil.
Can I bring us back to the domestic sphere for a moment — because the passage about Mrs Tulliver's influence is doing something extraordinary.
Eliot gives us this elaborate mechanical metaphor — the feather breaking the camel's back.
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back"
Credit or discredit — the ambivalence is exquisite.
The narrator refuses to assign blame to Mrs Tulliver — the camel's back was already breaking.
But notice: Mrs Tulliver only has this indirect effect because Tulliver sees her as the representative of the Dodson family.
He doesn't hear his wife — he hears a challenge to his male authority.
Yes — and Eliot marks that precisely.

The narrator says it was a guiding principle with Tulliver that the Dodsons should know they were not to domineer over him — specifically, that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female Dodsons.
Gender hierarchy and family pride are operating here as drivers of financial destruction.
And the Glegg episode shows us the same pride from the creditor's side.
Mrs Glegg is enjoying her own lofty magnanimity — preparing to be generous — and Tulliver demolishes it with a letter.
"he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
He is burning bridges he cannot afford to burn — and Eliot lets the comic timing carry the full weight of that irony.
There one must agree entirely.
Tulliver's letter to Mrs Glegg is an act of magnificent, self-defeating pride.
It has the shape of a tragic flaw — in the old Aristotelian sense — and Eliot renders it with the light touch of high comedy.
Johnson said that no man is a hypocrite in his pleasures — and one might add, no man is deceived in his pride.
Tulliver knows exactly what he is doing when he writes that letter.
What strikes me hearing all of this together is how Eliot refuses to give us a single cause for the collapse.
It is the law, the education system, the Dodson pride, Tulliver's own character — layered, interlocking.
And that final image — Maggie's voice breaking open the news to Tom — arrives with the simplicity of a verdict.
In our next segment, we'll look at how the Tulliver children carry the weight of that ruin forward — and what Eliot demands of them.

segments.title: Duty and Devotion: Sibling Bonds Fractured

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads — the education of Tom Tulliver, and the fracturing of his bond with Maggie.
We'll be asking how George Eliot uses the schoolroom — and the figure of Philip Wakem — to expose the machinery of class, prejudice, and misplaced duty.
Joining me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who brings an almost architectural eye to how Eliot builds her effects sentence by sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is, above all, a moral art — a study of character under pressure.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every classroom, every law office, every act of so-called kindness in a novel as a mechanism of class power.
Let's begin with Mr Stelling and his methods — or rather, his one method.
What Eliot does with Stelling is structurally extraordinary — she uses him to mount a satire that operates on at least three levels simultaneously.
There's the comic level — the beaver in a London flat, industriously damming a carpet.
But underneath that comedy is something chilling: a man who mistakes institutional habit for genuine vocation.
Listen to what Eliot does with his beliefs — she gives us the setup:
"He thought religion was a very excellent thing, and Aristotle a great authority, and deaneries and prebends useful institutions, and Great Britain the providential bulwark of Protestantism."
"He believed in all these things, as a Swiss hotel-keeper believes in the beauty of the scenery around him, and in the pleasure it gives to artistic visitors."
That comparison is devastating precisely because it's so polite.
Stelling doesn't disbelieve anything — he simply hasn't thought about any of it.
Eleanor is right that the satire is exquisitely poised, but I think we must take care not to let it obscure what Eliot is actually mourning here.
Stelling is not simply a comic figure — he is a figure of failed trust.
Mr Tulliver has placed his son in this man's hands with the most earnest hopes — and Stelling has defaulted on that trust through sheer incuriosity.
Eliot tells us, with barely concealed contempt, that
"Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver."
That word 'instilling' is doing terrible work — it implies liquid poured into a vessel, with no regard for the shape of the vessel at all.
The moral failure here is not political — it is a failure of attention, of the most basic human curiosity about the boy in front of him.
Edmund's point about trust is well made, but I'd press further: whose trust, and secured by what means?
Stelling isn't simply an inattentive individual — he's an institutional product, and Eliot shows us exactly how the institution functions.
Deaneries, prebends, Great Britain as providential bulwark — these aren't random items in a comic list.
They are the precise constellation of interests that the Anglican educational establishment exists to reproduce.
And Tom Tulliver, the miller's son, is simply the raw material on which this machinery is tested — with predictably grinding results.

Daniel's reading makes the metaphor chapter even more pointed — because Eliot then turns to examine Tom's actual intelligence, and the gap between what he can do and what Stelling can see is extraordinary.
She catalogues his perceptual gifts with real precision — the horses behind him, the stone thrown into a ripple, the squares drawn freehand on a slate.
And then she builds to this remarkable apostrophe — a direct address to Aristotle himself:

"O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor."
That pivot — from comedy to genuine pathos — is achieved in a single sentence, and it's breathtaking.
The passage on metaphor is, I think, among the finest things Eliot ever wrote — and it has a philosophical seriousness that the comic surface rather cunningly conceals.
She is making an epistemological argument: that all our ways of knowing a thing depend on the figurative language we choose, and that no figure is innocent.
The brain as stomach, the mind as white paper, the classics as plough and harrow — each metaphor licenses a different cruelty.
And behind it all is Tom — not stupid, but simply alien to the forms of abstraction that this particular institution has decided constitute intelligence.
What I find most striking is the narrator's aside — 'I say nothing against Mr Stelling's theory; if we are to have one regimen for all minds, his seems to me as good as any other.'
That conditional clause — 'if we are to have one regimen for all minds' — is where the real indictment lives.
Eliot is not merely criticising Stelling — she is questioning the premise that any single system of education can be just when the children entering it come from such radically different conditions.
Tom's 'stupidity' is produced by the system — it doesn't precede it.
And it's in this schoolroom that Tom meets Philip Wakem — a meeting that throws all of these questions about intelligence, prejudice, and class into sharp relief.
Eleanor, how does Eliot stage that first encounter between the two boys?
It's a masterclass in free indirect style — we're entirely inside Tom's perception, and the narrator lets that perception indict itself without comment.
Tom looks at Philip's face and finds it 'not a disagreeable face — very old-looking,' which is actually a concession of some interest from a boy determined to dislike him.
But then Eliot gives us the crux of his prejudice — and it's delivered with that perfectly calibrated satirical flatness:

"There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities."
'Public-spirited boys' — the irony is almost too good.
Tom's cruelty is dressed up as community virtue, which is exactly how such cruelties always present themselves.
One must be careful not to flatten Tom into a merely cruel boy — Eliot does not allow that either.
She notes, with considerable subtlety, that no face could be more unlike the ugly tailor's than this melancholy boy's — 'the brown hair round it waved and curled at the ends like a girl's.'
Tom is drawn to Philip against his will — and Eliot registers that gravitational pull with real tenderness.
The tragedy of this novel is not that Tom lacks feeling, but that his feelings are so entirely ungoverned by reflection.
I want to hold on to that detail about Philip's father — 'a vague notion that the deformity of Wakem's son had some relation to the lawyer's rascality.'

Tom has inherited from his father the belief that bodily difference and moral corruption are linked — and that this corruption is specifically associated with the class of men who use the law as an instrument of dispossession.
Philip is therefore doubly marked before Tom has spoken a word to him: as deformed, and as the son of the enemy.
Eliot is showing us how class hatred is transmitted through the body, lodged in the instincts of children who cannot yet name what they feel.
And yet Philip speaks — and what he says is wonderful.
Eliot gives him this extraordinary speech — part genuine idealism, part performance for Tom's benefit, which she flags with that delicious parenthetical.
He says — and the narrator's aside comes after:

"I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death."
And then: 'Philip, you perceive, was not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a sense of his mental superiority.'
'The well-made barbarian' — that phrase is doing so much work: Tom's physical confidence, Philip's compensatory intellectualism, and the entire question of what kind of excellence the world rewards.
The Greek fantasy is not merely showing off — it is a genuine index of Philip's longing.
He wants a world in which the body does not determine the man — where one might fight bravely and think beautifully and die with honour, regardless of one's physical form.
That is the dream that Tom, by virtue of his very wholeness, cannot imagine needing.
And it is also — though Philip does not yet know it — a dream that will be crushed not by Tom alone, but by everything Tom represents.
Philip's Greek fantasy is poignant — but Eliot is also clear-eyed about its social function.
Classical education — the very education that Tom is being ground against — is Philip's native element, the arena in which his disability becomes irrelevant and his intelligence sovereign.
So the schoolroom simultaneously destroys Tom and offers Philip a rare space of power.
That asymmetry is the seed of everything that follows between them — including the scene that Edmund has been assigned, in the grown-up confrontation over Maggie.
And that confrontation is where all of this crystallises — in the most brutal terms.
Edmund, the passage you've been sitting with — Tom's speech to Philip about Maggie — is one of the most uncomfortable in the whole novel.
Deeply uncomfortable — and I think deliberately so, in ways that resist any easy interpretation.
Tom speaks here as a man who is entirely convinced of his own rectitude — convinced that he is protecting his sister.
He says to Philip — and the voice must be heard at full force:
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you, — from making herself a laughing-stock, — from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son."
"You know well enough what sort of justice and cherishing you were preparing for her."
The word 'cherishing' — wielded with contempt — is the key.
Tom is accusing Philip of offering a love that would ultimately degrade Maggie — and he is not entirely wrong in his assessment of how Lawyer Wakem would respond.
But he is catastrophically wrong in his method — and in his absolute refusal to allow Maggie any voice in the matter.
Tom is right about one thing with terrible precision: Lawyer Wakem would indeed have flouted Maggie as 'not good enough.'
That is the class system speaking through Tom even as Tom thinks he is fighting it.
He has internalised Wakem senior's judgment — that the Tullivers are not good enough — and is now deploying it as a weapon against Philip.
And the last line — 'Come away, Maggie' — is perhaps the most chilling thing in the passage.
Three words, and Maggie's will is simply erased — not through violence but through the sheer weight of fraternal authority.
What strikes me is the syntactic structure of Tom's speech — the anaphora of 'I'll save her from.'
That repetition creates a rhetorical momentum that is almost hypnotic — Tom is performing heroic sacrifice to himself as much as to Philip.
And then that final declaration — 'I'm not to be imposed upon by fine words; I can see what actions mean.'
Tom believes himself the plain-speaking man of deeds — and Eliot allows that belief to stand long enough for us to see how lethal plain-speaking can be when it is also wrong.
And yet — I want to say this carefully — Eliot does not simply condemn Tom.
Everything Tom does here flows from his deepest nature — his loyalty, his sense of family honour, his genuine love for Maggie, however distorting that love has become.

Dr Johnson observed that the road to hell is paved with good intentions — but he might equally have noted that some of the most destructive acts in human history have been performed by people of genuine virtue.
That is Tom Tulliver's tragedy — and it is the tragedy Eliot insists we hold alongside our judgment of him.
Duty performed as cruelty, love expressed as erasure — and a childhood whose very structure prepared the ground for this moment.
That tension — between what Tom believes he is doing and what Eliot shows us he is actually doing — sits at the heart of everything we'll be discussing today.
Thank you all — we'll continue in just a moment.
Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Over the course of this episode, we're exploring George Eliot's extraordinary novel — its moral architecture, its social world, and the astonishing voice that holds everything together.
I'm joined today by three guests who bring very different lenses to the same rich material.

Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great subject is how writers construct their effects — the sentence, the image, the structural decision that makes a scene unforgettable.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance — by goodness, self-sacrifice, and the weakness of will.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — always asking what the institutions and the suffering tell us about the system that produced them.
We begin with something that underpins everything else in this novel: Eliot's narrative voice — its authority, its intimacy, and the extraordinary things it can do to a reader.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about specific moments where that voice does something remarkable — where shall we start?
I want to start with a moment that seems almost cinematically simple — Tom and Maggie, after the crisis at home, and Tom cannot weep.
Eliot gives us a physical image for what's happening inside him — and it's devastating.
She writes, and I want to read this carefully:
"He tightened his arm almost convulsively round Maggie as she sobbed, but his face looked rigid and tearless, his eyes blank, — as if a black curtain of cloud had suddenly fallen on his path."
That simile — the black curtain of cloud — is doing extraordinary work.
It isn't just grief — it's occlusion, a sudden blinding of the inner eye.
And notice that Tom holds Maggie convulsively — the body reaches out even when the mind has gone dark.
That's Eliot's omniscience at its best: she gives us what Tom cannot give himself — a name for what he's feeling.
That passage speaks, I think, to something more fundamental than technique — it speaks to the difference between Tom and Maggie as moral beings.
Tom has no distinct vision of their troubles — Eliot's phrase is exact.
He feels the crushing weight, but he cannot articulate it, cannot weep it out.
That limitation is not simply a flaw — it is the shape of his character, and the novel never quite lets us forget it.
The danger, as I see it, is that Eliot's narrator can be so sympathetic to Maggie that we read Tom too harshly — as mere obstacle rather than as a soul under pressure.
Edmund's point about vision is exactly right — but I'd push it further.
Tom's blankness is not simply temperament — it is the blankness of a young man who has been formed by a world that gives him no language for interiority.
And Eliot's narrator, crucially, supplies what that world withholds.
The black curtain of cloud — that image is the narrator's gift to Tom, not Tom's own.
That asymmetry — between what characters can name and what the narrating voice names for them — is, I'd argue, the novel's deepest political act.
Daniel has put his finger on something I find absolutely central — the narrator's role as the one who can see.
And there's a passage later in the novel where Eliot turns that gaze onto Maggie herself — with equal rigour, equal tenderness.
Maggie has retreated to her room after her terrible confrontation with Tom, and Eliot writes:
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict.
And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions."
That phrase — serene heights — is not just Maggie's aspiration, it's the narrator's ironic report of it.
Eliot loves Maggie too well to let her be simply noble — she shows us the gap between the ideal and the tumbling reality.
The irony you describe is, of course, what distinguishes a great novelist from a moralist.
Eliot does not simply endorse Maggie's spiritual programme — she subjects it to the test of experience.
And in that same passage, we are told her penitence and submission were constantly obstructed by a resentment she could not shake off as unjust.
That is the condition of moral seriousness — that goodness costs something, and is never quite clean.
What strikes me about that passage is what follows the reflection — the turn to Philip.
Eliot writes that her heart bled for Philip — and then the prose itself becomes physically urgent.
"It was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
Empathy, Eliot is insisting, is not a sentimental luxury — it has a physical cost.
And Philip is the figure the social order has broken most visibly — his exclusion from the Tulliver world is class violence with a civilised face.

I want to come back to something Edmund said about Eliot not simply endorsing Maggie — because there is one scene where the narrator does step back and let Maggie speak with full, almost unbearable authority.
The accusation she levels at Tom — and I think it is one of the great speeches in English fiction.
She tells him:
"If you were in fault ever, if you had done anything very wrong, I should be sorry for the pain it brought you; I should not want punishment to be heaped on you.
But you have always enjoyed punishing me; you have always been hard and cruel to me."
And then she goes further — right to the theological charge:
"You are nothing but a Pharisee. You thank God for nothing but your own virtues; you think they are great enough to win you everything else.
You have not even a vision of feelings by the side of which your shining virtues are mere darkness!"
The structure of that speech — from personal hurt, to moral accusation, to cosmic indictment — that is architecture.
It is a remarkable speech — and I would not diminish it.
But one must note that Maggie herself begins by saying: I know I've been wrong — often, continually.
The accusation is not a cry of innocence — it is a cry of someone who has accepted her own fault and demands the same of the person judging her.
That is the distinction between self-righteousness and moral seriousness — and Eliot draws it with a very fine pen.
What Maggie describes as Tom's cruelty — enjoying punishment, the hardness — these are not private failings.
They are the virtues the provincial commercial world rewards in men like Tom — discipline, severity, self-certainty.
Maggie calls him a Pharisee — and a Pharisee is someone whose goodness functions as power.
Tom's virtues are instruments of control, and they are perfectly calibrated to exclude her.
There is one more passage I want to bring in — because it speaks to everything we've been circling around: memory, damage, and the limit of repair.
Eliot opens a late chapter with one of the most quietly devastating sentences in the novel.
She's speaking of nature — the floods, the scarred hills — but the turn at the end is everything:
"Nature repairs her ravages, but not all. The uptorn trees are not rooted again; the parted hills are left scarred."
And then: "To the eyes that have dwelt on the past, there is no thorough repair."
Seven words that contain the whole novel's elegiac logic — memory as wound, not merely as sorrow.
Eliot gives the narrator's voice an authority here that isn't argument — it's verdict.
"To the eyes that have dwelt on the past" — that qualification changes everything.
It is not a statement about nature in the abstract — it is a statement about the condition of those who have loved and lost.
And there is something here very close to Burke's understanding of tradition — that what has been broken is not simply reconstructed, because the memory of wholeness makes the repair insufficient.
It is a profoundly conservative sentiment — and in Eliot's hands, entirely without consolation.
I'd read that passage against Edmund's grain — though not to dismiss him.
The hills bear the marks of the past rending — Eliot's word is rending, not simply time.
Something tore these hills — something violent made the scar.
For Maggie, the uprootings were not accidents of fate — they were the product of a world that systematically denied her the ground she needed to stand on.
The narrator's authority here is not merely elegiac — it is, I think, indicting.
Three very different readings of seven words — and all of them earned.

I think what Eliot's narrative voice achieves, in the passages Eleanor has brought us to, is precisely that: it can hold elegy, irony, and indictment in the same sentence without any one of them cancelling the others.
We'll be turning next to the social world the novel inhabits — the Tullivers and the Dodsons, commerce and respectability — and asking what Eliot is really doing with all that provincial furniture.

segments.title: The Social Order and Individual Struggle

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're looking at the social order and the individual struggle — and nowhere does Eliot anatomise that struggle more precisely than in the childhood chapters.
Maggie Tulliver, age eight or nine, is already navigating a world that has decided what she should be — and finding herself constitutionally unable to comply.
Eleanor Hartley is here — novelist, teacher of craft, and the person in this room most likely to catch Eliot doing something architecturally brilliant and feel personally grateful for it.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — retired Oxford don, defender of the moral imagination, and a man who believes character, not system, is the truest subject of fiction.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is with us — cultural historian, close reader of power, and someone who insists the novel knows more about class than its author sometimes admitted.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because what strikes me first about these passages is how Eliot renders jealousy in a child.
Yes — and the craft move Eliot makes here is almost disconcertingly precise.
She doesn't simply tell us Maggie is jealous of Lucy.
She shows us jealousy restructuring Maggie's perception — Lucy, who was innocent, becomes part of Tom's unkindness.
And then there's this extraordinary sentence — listen to how she sets it up:
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse is doing so much work there — it's innocence, smallness, defencelessness — exactly what Lucy is, exactly what makes Maggie's impulse so terrible and so human.
And Eliot doesn't flinch — Maggie actually wants to slap or pinch her, specifically to vex Tom.
That's not sentimentality about childhood — that's moral realism of the highest order.
Eleanor is absolutely right to call that realism — and I'd press the word even harder.
What Eliot is doing is tracing the genealogy of a moral failure — not excusing it, but illuminating it with full sympathy.
The sentence turns on that phrase 'as it was' — as it was, she was beginning to think cruel thoughts.
It's the narrator holding open the door between what Maggie might have been and what circumstances are making her.
This is the novel's great subject — not society's cruelty to Maggie, but Maggie's own nature under pressure.
That is what gives her tragedy its weight — the enemy is not only outside.
I want to take Edmund's point and push it into territory he may resist.
The enemy is not only outside, agreed — but we have to ask who constructed the inside.
Tom's indifference to Maggie, his sudden preference for Lucy — that's not some natural shift in a boy's affections.
It's the beginning of a gendered social script: Lucy is the approved model of femininity, and Tom is already being taught to value her over Maggie.
Maggie's violence — even in fantasy — is the direct product of that exclusion.
And what does she do with the unbearable pressure of that exclusion?
She runs — or imagines running — toward the only people who she thinks might receive her as she is.
And Eliot is devastatingly funny about how that fantasy is constructed.
The gypsy escape plan isn't just child's fancy — it's Maggie's entire epistemology on display.
She'll be received there on account of her superior knowledge — that's the logic, that's the consolation.
And then the narrator gives us this perfect diagnosis of how Maggie's mind actually works:
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
She knows the word 'polygamy' and has correctly deduced that 'poly' means 'many' — from the dictionary, mind you.
But she had no idea gypsies were not well supplied with groceries.
The comedy and the pathos are absolutely inseparable there — and that's Eliot at the height of her powers.
That phrase 'clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams' is one of the finest thumbnail portraits in the English novel.
And notice what Eliot refuses to do — she refuses to patronise Maggie by treating the fantasy as mere childish nonsense.
The gypsies were the only people Maggie could imagine who might value what she actually is.
That is a real insight into real suffering — dressed in comic costume, but genuine nonetheless.
And then Eliot turns the screw — the fantasy collapses into something approaching gothic horror.
The gypsies become cannibals in Maggie's imagination, and the old man becomes — possibly — the Devil himself.
And she wonders — with, Eliot tells us, a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded — whether, if the Devil were present, he would know her thoughts.
That is not satire at Maggie's expense — that is genuine sympathy with how a particular kind of mind under terror actually works.
I'd go further — that passage is also Eliot showing us what ideological formation looks like from the inside.
Maggie has absorbed a theology that makes the Devil omniscient — which means even her private thoughts aren't safe.
And look at the specific horror she's been given:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
Gradual cooking — it's almost parodic, except the terror is absolutely real to Maggie.
But the point is: this is what her culture has given her as a mental vocabulary for difference and danger.
The gypsies are the threatening other — even to an eight-year-old who thought she was running toward them as kindred spirits.
And yet — and this is where I want to bring in Tom — Maggie's mind, for all its wild mixture, is clearly extraordinary.
There's a passage about what happens to Tom after Maggie leaves Stelling's school that I find genuinely moving.
Oh, that passage — it's so beautifully calibrated.
Eliot is writing Tom's grief at losing Maggie, and she does it through a very particular detail.
Maggie had been pestering Stelling with questions about the Roman Empire — whether people really said those things in Latin.
And through that pestering, through Maggie's questions, something opened up for Tom:

"he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
'A dim understanding' — and Eliot calls it a 'luminous idea.' That irony is so gentle, so fond.
It's not mockery of Tom — it's grief, almost, that this is what passes for historical education in his world.
What moves me in that passage is the quiet reversal it enacts.
Tom, the one sent to school, has been learning less than Maggie, who reads dictionaries at home.
And yet the novel is perfectly clear — Tom is not stupid.
He misses her grievously — that word 'grievously' is doing real work — and his grief is legible as love.
The tragedy of Tom and Maggie is not that one is superior and the other is not — it's that they are differently formed by the same world, and those differences will eventually break them apart.
And that different formation is not accidental — it is systematically produced.
Tom gets the Eton Grammar and the epitomised history of the Jews — that's the education on offer for a boy of his class.
Maggie gets what she can scavenge from a dictionary and from asking questions no one wants her to ask.
And yet she's clearly the more intellectually alive of the two — Eliot makes sure we feel that without ever stating it flatly.
What the novel is quietly insisting is that the waste here — the waste of Maggie — is structural, not personal.
It is what the social order does, reliably, to people like her.
Structural waste — that's a formulation that's going to stay with me through the rest of this episode.
Eleanor, Edmund, Daniel — thank you.
We'll be moving next to the question of memory and belonging — and what it means for Maggie to love a world that cannot quite contain her.
We've arrived at the heart of this novel — and perhaps its most contested territory.
Tragedy, redemption, passion, and renunciation — the very architecture of Maggie Tulliver's inner life.
Eleanor, I want to start with you, because you've been circling a passage that I think cracks the novel wide open.
Yes — and it's a passage that announces itself almost as a theoretical statement about tragedy itself.
George Eliot is writing about Maggie as a small child, consumed by jealousy over little Lucy Deane.
And then she delivers this extraordinary sentence — half classical criticism, half devastating comedy.
"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only."
She even deploys the Greek — τι μέγεθος — the essential greatness of action that passion alone cannot supply.
And then the punchline: Maggie can only push Lucy into the cow-trodden mud.
It is comic — and yet it is the novel's tragic thesis stated in miniature.
What strikes me is the moral precision of that formulation.
Eliot is not saying Maggie's passion is insufficient — she is saying the world in which Maggie moves cannot receive it.
A girl with Maggie's interior life has been placed in a world governed by the Dodson code.
And what is that code? Eleanor touched the passages on it — and they are extraordinary.
The Dodsons' religion, as Eliot writes, was of a simple, semi-pagan kind.

"Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it,—if heresy properly means choice,—for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
Now that is devastating satire — but it is not contempt.
Eliot understands the Dodsons from the inside — she grants them their dignity even while she dissects their limitations.
Edmund is right that there's no contempt — but I'd press on what that code actually does.
The Dodson religion of respectability is inseparable from property, from inheritance, from the correct distribution of shoebuckles.
It is a moral system that has organized itself entirely around the preservation of economic standing.
And into that world steps Maggie — whose inner life cannot be valued by any of its metrics.
Her passion is real, her intelligence is real — and the system has no place for either.
And that is precisely where Thomas à Kempis enters — at Maggie's moment of most acute dispossession.
She picks up this old, clumsy book — with its corners turned down, its markings made by a hand now forever quiet.
The gothic detail of that anonymous hand is doing so much work — she is not alone in her suffering.
And then she reads where that quiet hand pointed — and the voice out of the middle ages speaks directly to her condition.

"Know that the love of thyself doth hurt thee more than anything in the world.... If thou seekest this or that, and wouldst be here or there to enjoy thy own will and pleasure, thou shalt never be quiet nor free from care."
It is counsel for renunciation — and Maggie receives it like a revelation.
And what Eliot does with that revelation is quite extraordinarily honest.
She shows us Maggie in a state of genuine spiritual illumination — and simultaneously shows us that the illumination is incomplete.
The narrator tells us plainly what Maggie has not yet perceived — that renunciation remains sorrow, though a sorrow borne willingly.
But Maggie, for now, is in ecstasy — and Eliot renders that ecstasy with full tenderness.
That is not irony at Maggie's expense — it is the deepest moral sympathy.
I find myself moved by that reading of Edmund's — and also troubled by it.
Because what Maggie discovers, let's be clear, is a spiritual path that promises peace through self-erasure.
Eliot describes it with such precision — the flash of insight, like the suddenly apprehended solution of a problem.

"It flashed through her like the suddenly apprehended solution of a problem, that all the miseries of her young life had come from fixing her heart on her own pleasure, as if that were the central necessity of the universe."
Now — Eliot is not endorsing this as a sufficient answer.
The novel will go on to test renunciation — and find it wanting, in precisely the way the passionate little girl found tragedy wanting.
The structure of the novel echoes itself — and that echo is devastating.
That structural echo is exactly right — and it's what makes Eliot a novelist rather than a moralist.
The passionate child who cannot perform tragedy — and the passionate young woman who cannot perform sainthood.
Maggie's tragedy is that she is always too much for the forms available to her.
And Eliot honours that excess rather than correcting it.
Too much for the forms available to her — that may be the most precise summary of Maggie Tulliver I've ever heard.
What this conversation has shown is how completely Eliot holds all of it at once — the comedy, the tragedy, the satire, and the tenderness.
Eleanor, Edmund, Daniel — this has been a genuinely illuminating hour, and I'm grateful to all three of you.
And to our listeners: The Mill on the Floss rewards every return visit — perhaps especially now.
Thank you for joining us on The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

Poor child! it was very early for her to know one of those supreme moments in
life when all we have hoped or delighted in, all we can dread or endure, falls
away from our regard as insignificant; is lost, like a trivial memory, in that
simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to
us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish.
c21:p15.summary: The narrator reflects on how Maggie's supreme moment—seeing her father's helplessness—dissolves all other concerns into a single primitive devotion.

“Say no more, Tom, say no more; I’ve had enough for this day. Give
me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be
young again—this world’s been too many for me.”

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”
c37:p53.summary: Tom insists Maggie must put her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words of renunciation, claiming he cannot trust her, that she lacks consistency, and that while he has been working to pay their father's debts and restore family respectability, she has done everything to destroy both.
c37:p53.best_quote: I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both

c14:p11.text:
Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”
c14:p11.summary: Humiliated by repeated failures, Tom resorts to prayer, adding petitions for Latin and Euclid to his nightly prayers, showing his desperation and underlying sensitivity.
c14:p11.best_quote: and please to make me always remember my Latin

c14:p58.text:
Maggie found the Latin Grammar quite soothing after her mathematical
mortification; for she delighted in new words, and quickly found that there was
an English Key at the end, which would make her very wise about Latin, at
slight expense. She presently made up her mind to skip the rules in the Syntax,
the examples became so absorbing. These mysterious sentences, snatched from an
unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown
plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her
imagination, and were all the more fascinating because they were in a peculiar
tongue of their own, which she could learn to interpret. It was really very
interesting, the Latin Grammar that Tom had said no girls could learn; and she
was proud because she found it interesting. The most fragmentary examples were
her favourites.  Mors omnibus est communis  would have been jejune, only
she liked to know the Latin; but the fortunate gentleman whom every one
congratulated because he had a son “endowed with  such  a
disposition” afforded her a great deal of pleasant conjecture, and she
was quite lost in the “thick grove penetrable by no star,” when Tom
called out,—
c14:p58.summary: Maggie discovers joy in the Latin Grammar's fragmentary examples, finding them imaginatively stimulating and delighting in the foreign language's mysterious beauty.
c14:p58.best_quote: These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her imagination

c18:p26.text:
“One—two,” said Tom, resolutely, though at “two”
his wrist trembled a little. “Three” came more slowly, and with it
the sword swung downward, and Maggie gave a loud shriek. The sword had fallen,
with its edge on Tom’s foot, and in a moment after he had fallen too.
Maggie leaped from the bed, still shrieking, and immediately there was a rush
of footsteps toward the room. Mr Stelling, from his upstairs study, was the
first to enter. He found both the children on the floor. Tom had fainted, and
Maggie was shaking him by the collar of his jacket, screaming, with wild eyes.
She thought he was dead, poor child! and yet she shook him, as if that would
bring him back to life. In another minute she was sobbing with joy because Tom
opened his eyes. She couldn’t sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it
seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive.
c18:p26.summary: The sword falls on Tom's foot, causing him to faint; Maggie screams and shakes him in terror, believing him dead, until he revives; her overwhelming relief reveals the depth of her love for her brother.
c18:p26.best_quote: She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive.

“It’s about Philoctetes, the lame man I was telling you of
yesterday,” he answered, resting his head on his hand, and looking at her
as if he were not at all sorry to be interrupted. Maggie, in her absent way,

c19:p18.summary: Philip asks whether Maggie would love him as well as Tom if he were her brother, a question laden with the subtext of his physical deformity and desire for affection.

c19:p27.text: “Oh, yes, I should think so,” said Maggie, laughing.
c19:p27.summary: Philip confesses his deep and enduring affection for Maggie, stating he will remember her always and, in unhappiness, will think of her and wish for a sister with her dark eyes.

c19:p31.text:

c20:p18.text:
“Yes,” said Maggie, again faintly. Then, urged to fuller speech by
Tom’s freedom from apprehension, she said loudly and rapidly, as if the
words  would  burst from her: “Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and
the land and everything; he will have nothing left.”
